# Nadi42

Nadi42 is a 42-day postpartum continuity platform that turns missed warning signs into actionable follow-up for mothers, families, ASHAs, and Primary Health Centres (PHCs).

Most maternal-health tools focus on pregnancy and delivery. Once a mother goes home, the care loop often disappears. Nadi42 focuses on those first 42 days after childbirth, detecting risk early and making sure it is actually followed up on rather than simply logged.

The product's guiding flow is simple: a mother goes home, Nadi42 checks in with her, risk is detected, her family or ASHA is alerted, care is connected, and the follow-up is closed.

## Overview

Nadi42 is a single responsive web application built around three role-based dashboards. Mothers use it to complete daily check-ins, report symptoms, and track their recovery. ASHAs and health workers use it to monitor the mothers assigned to them, receive risk alerts, and log follow-up visits. PHC supervisors use it to view population-level trends, monitor high-risk cases, and track how well follow-ups are being completed.

The core idea behind the product is continuity of care, not another pregnancy-tracking app.

---

## User Roles

![The three Nadi42 dashboards: Mother, ASHA / Health Worker, and PHC / Supervisor](data:image/png;base64,)

**Mother.** Completes daily or periodic check-ins, reports symptoms, views her recovery timeline, requests help when needed, sees upcoming follow-ups, and receives simple guidance in her preferred language.

**ASHA / Health Worker.** Sees her assigned mothers and their current risk status, is notified of missed check-ins, receives real-time alerts when a mother's risk level changes, can call or message a mother directly, records the outcome of each follow-up, and escalates serious cases to the PHC.

**PHC / Supervisor.** Views a population-level dashboard, monitors high-risk and unresolved cases, tracks how completely follow-ups are being carried out, and identifies gaps in geographic coverage or service delivery.

---

## The Nadi Risk Loop

![The Nadi Risk Loop: check-in leads to a rules-based risk classification of Green, Amber, or Red, then ASHA notification, follow-up, PHC escalation, and case closure](data:image/png;base64,)

This is the centerpiece of the product, and every other feature exists to support it. A mother completes a daily or scheduled check-in. Her responses are passed through a risk engine built on deterministic rules rather than an AI model, which classifies her status as Green, Amber, or Red. A Green result means monitoring simply continues. An Amber result means a follow-up is required. A Red result triggers an urgent escalation. Whenever a case is Amber or Red, the assigned ASHA is notified, she carries out the follow-up action, and if necessary escalates further to the PHC. Once the issue has been addressed, the case is marked closed.

Keeping the risk engine rule-based rather than AI-driven is a deliberate safety choice: it keeps the clinical decision auditable and predictable. Artificial intelligence is used only to assist communication, such as translation, summarization, and message generation, and never to make the underlying clinical call.

It is worth noting that any clinical rules used in a real deployment would need to be validated by qualified maternal-health professionals and aligned with applicable Indian clinical protocols. The current logic is a simplified version built for a hackathon and demonstration setting.

## Tech Stack

**Frontend.** Built with Next.js and TypeScript, styled with Tailwind CSS and shadcn/ui components, animated with Framer Motion, and using React Hook Form together with Zod for form handling and validation. Charts are rendered with Recharts, and icons come from Lucide.

**Backend.** Implemented using Next.js API routes and route handlers, backed by a MongoDB database accessed through Mongoose or the native MongoDB Node.js driver. Authentication is handled through NextAuth.js or a custom JWT-based layer. Real-time updates are powered by Socket.io or MongoDB Change Streams. File storage, where needed, is provided by Cloudinary or AWS S3.

**External Services.** Twilio powers SMS and WhatsApp check-in prompts and ASHA alerts. Google Maps powers nearest-facility routing when a case is escalated. OpenAI is used optionally for local-language interpretation and note summarization.

**Analytics.** Product analytics are tracked using PostHog.

**Deployment.** The application is deployed on Vercel, with MongoDB Atlas serving as the hosted database.

---

## Project Structure

The application follows a standard Next.js App Router layout. Authentication-related pages such as login, signup, and onboarding are grouped together. Each user role has its own dedicated section: mothers have dashboard, check-in, timeline, and help pages; ASHAs have dashboard, mothers, alerts, and cases pages; PHC supervisors have dashboard, cases, and analytics pages. API routes are organized by function, covering risk calculation, notifications, AI-assisted features, and maps.

Shared UI elements live in a components directory, split into general UI primitives, charts, forms, check-in components, alerts, maps, and navigation. Core business logic sits in a library directory, which includes the database connection helper and Mongoose models, the risk engine, Twilio integration, maps integration, OpenAI integration, and analytics helpers. Custom React hooks handle mother data, check-in state, and realtime case updates. TypeScript types are defined for mothers, check-ins, and cases, and constants such as check-in questions and risk thresholds are kept in their own directory. A seed script populates the database with demo data, and static assets such as icons and illustrations live in the public directory.

---

## Database Design

Nadi42 uses MongoDB collections rather than relational tables, with relationships modeled through object ID references. Frequently read summary fields, such as a mother's current risk level, are denormalized directly onto her document so that dashboards can be read quickly without extra lookups.

The **users** collection stores login credentials, role (mother, ASHA, or PHC), name, phone number, preferred language, and account creation date.

The **mothers** collection links each mother to her user account, her assigned ASHA, and her assigned PHC facility, along with her delivery date, geographic location, current risk level, and the timestamp of her last check-in.

The **checkins** collection records each individual check-in submission, including symptoms such as bleeding severity, fever, headache, vision changes, emotional state, and feeding difficulty, along with the resulting risk level and timestamp.

The **cases** collection tracks a risk event from creation to resolution, recording which mother and check-in triggered it, its current risk level and status, what caused it, which ASHA it is assigned to, and when it was created or resolved.

The **followups** collection records the follow-up actions taken against a case, including the responsible ASHA, when the follow-up was scheduled and completed, any notes taken, and its current status.

The **notifications** collection stores messages sent to users, including their type, content, read status, and creation time.

The **facilities** collection stores PHCs and hospitals, including their name, type, geographic location, and contact number.

To keep dashboard queries fast, indexes are recommended on the ASHA and PHC references within the mothers collection, on the geographic location fields for both mothers and facilities to support nearest-facility queries, on check-in records by mother and date, and on cases by status, risk level, and assigned ASHA.

Conceptually, the data flows from a mother, to her check-ins and the risk results they produce, to the cases those results generate, which involve her ASHA and PHC, and finally to the follow-ups that lead to resolution.

![Continuity relationship: Mother leads to Check-ins, which lead to Cases involving ASHA and PHC, which lead to Follow-ups](data:image/png;base64,)

## Getting Started

Before running the project, you will need Node.js version 18 or later, a MongoDB Atlas cluster or local MongoDB instance, a Twilio account for SMS and WhatsApp alerts, a Google Maps API key, and optionally an OpenAI API key.

To get started, clone the repository, install dependencies, copy the example environment file into a local environment file and fill in your credentials, run the database seed script to populate demo data, and then start the development server. Once running, the application will be available locally on port 3000.

---

## Environment Configuration

The application requires configuration values for the MongoDB connection string, authentication secret and URL, Twilio account credentials and phone number, a Google Maps API key, an optional OpenAI API key, and PostHog analytics credentials. These should be provided through a local environment file that is never committed to version control.

---

## External Integrations

**Twilio** sends daily check-in prompts to mothers over SMS or WhatsApp and delivers real-time risk alerts to ASHAs.

**Google Maps** powers the nearest-facility escalation screen that appears when a case turns Red, providing directions along with distance and estimated time of arrival from the mother's location to the nearest PHC.

**OpenAI**, used optionally, converts local-language responses from mothers into structured symptom signals and generates concise case summaries for ASHAs. It is important to note that AI never decides a mother's risk level; that decision always comes from the deterministic rules engine.

---

## Demo Accounts and Seed Data

The seed script populates the database with a demonstration population of 428 mothers, of whom 351 are classified Green, 56 Amber, and 21 Red. It also creates 391 check-ins for the current day, 37 pending follow-ups, and 34 resolved cases.

Three demo accounts are provided for walkthroughs: one for a mother, one for an ASHA, and one for a PHC supervisor. A dedicated demo mother, referred to as "Meena" and on postpartum day 11, is seeded specifically to walk through the full red-risk journey from check-in, through risk detection, ASHA alert, map-based escalation, follow-up, and finally case closure.

---

## Roadmap and Scope

Several features are deliberately excluded from the initial build so the team can focus on doing the core loop well. These include full pregnancy tracking, a baby growth tracker, a large article or content library, complex appointment booking, payments, social community features, a doctor marketplace, wearable device integrations, machine-learning-based diagnosis, and multi-language support beyond one or two languages at launch.

The goal of the minimum viable product is to execute the Detect, Alert, Connect, Follow Up, and Close loop extremely well, rather than to build a broad and half-finished platform.
